value.overview: The Gray-breasted Wood-Wren (Henicorhina leucophrys) is a small, active wren of humid mountain forests from Mexico south through Central America and the Andes of South America. It usually stays in dense understory vegetation, where it searches among moss, ferns, roots, fallen branches, and tangled plants. Its rich, ringing song is often easier to detect than the bird itself. In Costa Rica, it is a familiar resident of suitable highland forests and forest edges.
value.classification: The Gray-breasted Wood-Wren belongs to the wren family Troglodytidae and the genus Henicorhina. It is part of a species complex with several geographically distinct forms across its broad range.
value.identification: This compact wren has gray underparts, an olive-brown back and wings, a warm brown rump, and a long, often slightly cocked tail. The face is marked by a conspicuous pale or whitish eyebrow stripe, with darker shading through the eye. It commonly moves through dense vegetation in short hops and may flick or raise its tail. In Costa Rica, its repeated, musical song is a useful way to locate this otherwise secretive bird.
value.rangeHabitat: The species has a broad distribution from southern Mexico through Central America to the Andes of northern and western South America. In Costa Rica, it occurs mainly in the cooler highlands and montane regions, including suitable habitats on both Caribbean and Pacific slopes. It uses humid montane evergreen forest, cloud forest, ravines, dense second growth, forest borders, and mossy understory, generally at middle to high elevations. It can persist in partially modified landscapes when dense, shaded vegetation remains.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident and non-migratory. Costa Rican populations are year-round residents of highland and montane habitats, although individuals may make local movements along elevational gradients or between nearby forest patches.
value.breeding: Breeding biology varies across its extensive range, but the species typically builds a covered or domed nest in dense vegetation, a cavity, bank, root mass, or other protected site close to the ground. The nest is made from materials such as moss, leaves, grass, and plant fibers. Pairs are territorial and may cooperate in nest defense and care of young. In Costa Rica, breeding can occur during the local wet-season breeding period, but timing varies by elevation and region.
value.dietFeeding: The Gray-breasted Wood-Wren feeds mainly on small invertebrates, including insects, spiders, and other arthropods. It forages actively but discreetly in the shaded understory, probing leaf litter, moss, bromeliads, dead leaves, roots, and tangled branches. It usually remains close to cover and may forage alone, in pairs, or in mixed-species flocks. Its rounded wings and short flights suit movement through dense vegetation rather than open spaces.
value.behavior: This wren is secretive, energetic, and strongly vocal. It often travels through dense understory in pairs or family groups, using short hops and brief flights while keeping low in vegetation. Its loud, complex song may be delivered from a concealed perch and is important in territorial communication. The species can be difficult to see even when it is nearby. It commonly holds its tail elevated and responds to neighboring birds with repeated calls or song.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is reported as decreasing, although the species remains widespread and locally common in suitable mountain forest habitat.
